cases.name: clean-first-enquiry
cases.existing: No contacts in the book at all.
cases.why: Nothing exists to match, so the resolver creates a record rather than erroring — the baseline every other case builds on.

cases.name: mobile-national-spaced-format
cases.existing: One contact, Jane Citizen, phone_e164 '+61412345678', no email.
cases.why: The trunk-zero rule collapses '0412 345 678' to the identical E.164 key, and a single clean phone hit with a consistent name is exactly the dedupe CLAUDE.md section 4 prescribes.

cases.name: mobile-plus61-inbound
cases.existing: Jane Citizen created from raw phone '0412 345 678', stored phone_e164 '+61412345678'.
cases.why: Normalisation is symmetric — the national and the +61 written forms collapse to one key, mirroring the existing 'matches on phone even when typed in different formats' test.

cases.name: mobile-61-without-plus
cases.existing: Jane Citizen with phone_e164 '+61412345678'.
cases.why: A leading 61 with no '+' (typical of portal feeds and copy-paste) is the same country-coded number, and toE164 already prefixes the '+' for it.

cases.name: mobile-parenthesised-hyphenated
cases.existing: Jane Citizen with phone_e164 '+61412345678'.
cases.why: Parentheses, hyphens and grouping are presentation only — the digit string is 0412345678, the same key.

cases.name: mobile-with-annotation
cases.existing: Jane Citizen with phone_e164 '+61412345678'.
cases.why: Human annotations contribute no digits, so normalisation strips them and the key still matches cleanly.

cases.name: mobile-plus61-with-trunk-zero
cases.existing: Jane Citizen with phone_e164 '+61412345678'.
cases.why: The parenthesised trunk zero in this very common written form must be dropped once +61 is present — a naive normaliser yields '+610412345678' and silently duplicates every such enquiry.

cases.name: landline-national-format
cases.existing: Raj Patel, phone_e164 '+61881234567', email raj.patel@example.com.
cases.why: '08 8123 4567' normalises to the identical E.164 landline key and the name agrees, so this is a safe single-candidate match.

cases.name: landline-international-format
cases.existing: Raj Patel created from raw phone '08 8123 4567', stored phone_e164 '+61881234567'.
cases.why: Both landline spellings collapse to '+61881234567', proving format symmetry holds for landlines as well as mobiles.

cases.name: landline-shared-household
cases.existing: Raj Patel with phone_e164 '+61881234567' and email raj.patel@example.com.
cases.why: A landline is a household key, not a personal one — the differing name and email say this is plausibly a different person at the same number, which is precisely what the merge review queue exists to decide.

cases.name: landline-matches-two-contacts
cases.existing: Two open contacts, Raj Patel and Meera Patel, both holding phone_e164 '+61881234567'.
cases.why: One key returning two candidates can never be auto-picked — choosing either would be an unauthorised identity decision.

cases.name: uk-international-number
cases.existing: Oliver Hart (overseas investor), phone_e164 '+447911123456', no email.
cases.why: toE164 preserves an explicit foreign country code untouched, and exact E.164 equality is as safe for +44 as for +61 — normalisation must never force-prefix +61 onto an already-international number.

cases.name: junk-phone-only
cases.existing: A contact also named Somebody Keen, with a real phone and email.
cases.why: 'call me' yields no digits so toE164 returns null, leaving no dedupe key at all, and the coinciding name is never a match signal.

cases.name: junk-phone-but-valid-email
cases.existing: Jane Citizen with email_normalised 'jane@example.com'.
cases.why: The unparseable phone degrades to null and is simply ignored — one key failing to parse must not poison the clean email match.

cases.name: local-number-without-area-code
cases.existing: Raj Patel with phone_e164 '+61881234567'.
cases.why: Eight digits with no area code cannot be completed to E.164 without guessing ('+6181234567' is not '+61881234567'), and a fabricated key must match nothing rather than fuzzily hit the landline.

cases.name: plus-addressed-email
cases.existing: Jane Citizen with email_normalised 'jane@example.com' (raw 'jane@example.com').
cases.why: normaliseEmail strips plus-addressing before comparison, so a duplicate cannot hide behind a tag — the convention the existing createContact test already fixes.

cases.name: email-case-insensitive
cases.existing: Jane Citizen with email_normalised 'jane@example.com'.
cases.why: Email comparison is case-insensitive end to end — local part and domain are lower-cased at write time and at lookup time.

cases.name: email-trailing-dot-and-space
cases.existing: Jane Citizen with email_normalised 'jane@example.com'.
cases.why: Policy: trailing whitespace is a paste artefact and a trailing domain dot is the DNS root label — both denote the same mailbox, so normalisation strips them (note current normaliseEmail trims the space but keeps the dot, so this case pins the fix).

cases.name: gmail-dot-variant
cases.existing: John Smith with email_normalised 'johnsmith@gmail.com'.
cases.why: Policy: Google documents that dots in gmail.com/googlemail.com locals are ignored, so both spellings are provably one mailbox — strip dots for those two domains only, making this as safe as the plus-address stripping already in place.

cases.name: non-gmail-dot-variant
cases.existing: John Smith with email_normalised 'johnsmith@bigpond.com'.
cases.why: Outside Gmail's documented behaviour, RFC 5321 makes the local part opaque and dotted/undotted can be two real mailboxes owned by two real people, so no key matches — and a near-miss on a non-guaranteed transformation is not grounds for a review either.

cases.name: email-match-name-wildly-different
cases.existing: Annette D'Souza with email_normalised 'dsouza.family@example.com'.
cases.why: An exact email key with a flatly conflicting name is the shared-family-mailbox pattern — a plausible match that would be unsafe to auto-merge, so it goes to the review queue.

cases.name: email-match-nickname-variant
cases.existing: Joanne Nguyen with email_normalised 'joanne.n@example.com'.
cases.why: The key matches and a diminutive of the recorded first name is corroboration rather than conflict — treating every nickname as a different person would fork records constantly.

cases.name: mobile-match-new-email-same-name
cases.existing: Jane Citizen with phone_e164 '+61412345678' and email_normalised 'jane@oldisp.com.au'.
cases.why: An exact personal-mobile key with a consistent name is a safe match; the unfamiliar email is a proposed update for the confirm queue (rule 5), not evidence of a different person.

cases.name: mobile-match-different-person-details
cases.existing: Jane Citizen with phone_e164 '+61412345678' and email 'jane@oldisp.com.au'.
cases.why: Mobiles are recycled and shared within families, so an exact number carrying a conflicting name AND a conflicting email is plausible-but-unsafe — review, never auto-merge.

cases.name: email-match-unknown-phone
cases.existing: Jane Citizen with email_normalised 'jane@example.com' and phone_e164 '+61412345678'; no contact holds +61455000222.
cases.why: One key hitting cleanly while the other key matches nothing is a safe match — the new number is additional data to propose, not a reason for doubt.

cases.name: both-keys-same-record
cases.existing: Jane Citizen with email_normalised 'jane@example.com' and phone_e164 '+61412345678'.
cases.why: Both normalised keys agree on the same contact — the strongest possible signal, so it must resolve even though both inbound values are format variants.

cases.name: email-hits-A-phone-hits-B
cases.existing: Record A holds email_normalised 'jane@example.com'; a different record B (Marco Rossi) holds phone_e164 '+61498765432'.
cases.why: Two keys naming two different contacts is a conflict only a person can resolve — and is often the moment an existing duplicate pair is first discovered.

cases.name: two-records-share-normalised-email
cases.existing: Two open contacts both normalising to 'jane@example.com' — an unresolved duplicate pair with an open merge review (the schema deliberately allows this).
cases.why: Picking either record would silently pre-empt the open human decision the merge review exists for, so the enquiry attaches to the review instead.

cases.name: phone-tiebreak-among-duplicates-forbidden
cases.existing: Records A and B both hold email_normalised 'jane@example.com'; only A also holds phone_e164 '+61412345678'.
cases.why: Using the phone to pick A out of an unresolved duplicated-email pair is an auto-merge in disguise — the tie-break is the human's call, not the resolver's.

cases.name: same-name-only-never-matches
cases.existing: Sarah Jones with a completely different email and phone; neither inbound key matches any contact.
cases.why: Section 4 dedupes on normalised email and E.164 phone only — a shared name is demographic coincidence, must NEVER auto-match, and should not even queue a review or every second Sarah Jones buries the real duplicates.

cases.name: no-keys-at-all
cases.existing: Alex Wu with full email and phone details.
cases.why: Empty and whitespace-only strings normalise to null exactly like absent fields, and with both keys null the only remaining signal is the name, which never matches.

cases.name: tombstoned-record-match
cases.existing: Jane Citizen, email_normalised 'jane@example.com', tombstoned_at set after a privacy deletion request, do_not_contact true.
cases.why: Identity survives a privacy mark — resolving to the tombstoned record lets downstream enforcement refuse activity and honour do-not-contact, whereas creating a fresh record would launder the removal request into a contactable duplicate.

cases.name: merged-loser-email-match
cases.existing: Contact L (holding email_normalised 'dana@example.com') was merged into contact S: L has merged_into_id = S and is tombstoned; S survives.
cases.why: The one-hop merged_into_id pointer must be followed and S returned — L is superseded, not a separate person, and logging against L is refused anyway per the superseded-record tests.

cases.name: merged-loser-and-survivor-both-hit
cases.existing: Survivor S holds email_normalised 'dana.new@example.com'; loser L (merged into S) still holds phone_e164 '+61433900123'.
cases.why: After pointer resolution both keys collapse to the single contact S, so what looks like a two-candidate conflict is one person — candidates must be deduplicated by resolved id before the ambiguity check.

cases.name: whitespace-and-typography-in-name
cases.existing: Zoe O'Brien with email_normalised 'zoe@example.com' (plain ASCII name, straight apostrophe).
cases.why: The email key decides; names are compared only for conflict detection and only after trimming, whitespace-collapsing and diacritic/quote folding, so typography is never a conflict.

cases.name: nfc-vs-nfd-unicode-name
cases.existing: José García (name stored NFC-composed) with phone_e164 '+61412700800'; the inbound name arrives NFD-decomposed from a web form.
cases.why: NFC and NFD are byte-different but visually identical, so names must be unicode-normalised before comparison — an accent encoding must never turn a clean phone match into a false conflict.

cases.name: secondary-email-match
cases.existing: Jane Citizen with primary email_normalised 'jane@example.com' and secondary_email 'j.citizen@work.example.com'.
cases.why: The secondary email column exists precisely because one person owns several mailboxes, so a normalised hit on it is the same single-candidate key match as a primary hit.

missing: Tombstoned record holds the matching key: the stated rule 'tombstoned records never match' has zero coverage — need a case where the only email/phone hit is a tombstoned contact and the verdict is 'new' (not 'existing', not 'ambiguous').
Key shared by one tombstoned record and one open record: the tombstone must be invisible, leaving a clean single-candidate 'existing' match on the open record rather than a two-candidate 'ambiguous'.

Enquiry key matches a record that was merged away: the stated rule 'merged records resolve to their survivor' has zero coverage — need a case asserting the resolver returns the survivor as 'existing', never the merged-away id.
Chained merges (A merged into B, B merged into C): resolution must follow the chain transitively to the final survivor without looping.

Junk email handling is entirely untested — every junk-input case is phone-side. Need the symmetric pair: junk email (e.g. 'n/a', 'none supplied') + valid matching phone must still resolve 'existing' (bad email must not poison the phone key), and junk email + no phone yields 'new'.

Portal/role email blocklist: AU portal feeds (realestate.com.au, Domain) inject shared noreply/reply-relay addresses, and offices share info@ mailboxes — without an exclusion list one such email silently funnels every enquirer into a single contact. Need cases asserting these addresses are never used as dedupe keys.
Two open contacts sharing the same MOBILE (e.g. a couple sharing a phone): the one-key-two-candidates 'ambiguous' branch is only tested on a landline — pin that it is key-type-agnostic.

Wrong-length AU numbers (9-digit '0412 345 67', 11-digit '0412 345 6789'): toE164 must return null rather than a padded/truncated fabricated key — only the 8-digit missing-area-code shape is currently tested.
13/1300/1800 business numbers: shared non-personal numbers common in real-estate signatures — define policy (they should never be a personal dedupe key / never auto-match).
gmail.com <-> googlemail.com cross-domain equivalence: the stated Gmail policy names both domains, but no case pins that john.smith@googlemail.com matches johnsmith@gmail.com.

Plus-addressed email with a CONFLICTING name (e.g. 'Bruce Chen' sending from annette+agent@...): should follow the same shared-mailbox 'ambiguous' path as email-match-name-wildly-different. Also decide whether plus-stripping should be provider-scoped: stripping '+tag' universally on example.com contradicts the RFC-5321-opacity rationale the table itself uses to forbid dot-stripping on bigpond.com — one policy or the other must give.

Enquiry attaching to an open merge review via the PHONE key: review-attachment is only tested through a shared email (two-records-share-normalised-email) — pin that the attach-to-review behaviour is key-agnostic.

Foreign number typed in national format without '+' (e.g. UK '07911 123456'): naive AU coercion fabricates '+617911123456' — normalisation must validate against the AU numbering plan and yield null rather than a bogus key that can silently collide.
The final case 'same-name-only-never-matches' arrived truncated mid-fixture ('neither inbo...') — confirm it ends with expect 'new' and that no review is raised on name coincidence alone.
